**Reconstruct Itinerary** · Hard

You get a list of plane tickets, each a pair `[from, to]` of airport codes. One traveller owns all of them and starts at `"JFK"`. Arrange the tickets into a single trip that uses **every ticket exactly once**. When several trips are possible, return the one that is smallest in dictionary order when the airport codes are read as one sequence. At least one valid trip is guaranteed to exist.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ tickets.length ≤ 300
- each code is 3 uppercase letters; the same ticket may appear more than once

**Example 1**

```graph
JFK -> MUC
MUC -> LHR
LHR -> SFO
SFO -> SJC
```

Input: `tickets = [["MUC","LHR"],["JFK","MUC"],["SFO","SJC"],["LHR","SFO"]]`
Output: `["JFK","MUC","LHR","SFO","SJC"]`
Only one chain of flights uses all four tickets.

**Example 2**

```graph
JFK -> SFO
JFK -> ATL
SFO -> ATL
ATL -> JFK
ATL -> SFO
```

Input: `tickets = [["JFK","SFO"],["JFK","ATL"],["SFO","ATL"],["ATL","JFK"],["ATL","SFO"]]`
Output: `["JFK","ATL","JFK","SFO","ATL","SFO"]`
`["JFK","SFO","ATL","JFK","ATL","SFO"]` also uses every ticket, but it is larger in dictionary order (`SFO` > `ATL` at position 2).

**Example 3**
Input: `tickets = [["JFK","KUL"],["JFK","NRT"],["NRT","JFK"]]` → Output: `["JFK","NRT","JFK","KUL"]` (going to `KUL` first is smaller but strands the other tickets)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/reconstruct-flight-path) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/reconstruct-itinerary/)

**Min Cost to Connect All Points** · Medium

You get `n` distinct points on a 2-D plane, `points[i] = [x, y]`. Joining two points costs their Manhattan distance, `|x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|`. Return the minimum total cost to join the points so that every point can reach every other point through the chosen connections (each pair connected by exactly one route).

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000
- −10⁶ ≤ x, y ≤ 10⁶; all points distinct

**Example 1**

```graph
A -- B : 4
B -- D : 3
D -- E : 4
B -- C : 9
caption: A(0,0) B(2,2) C(3,10) D(5,2) E(7,0): cheapest connections
```

Input: `points = [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]]`
Output: `20`
4 + 3 + 4 + 9 = 20, and no other set of connections that links all five points is cheaper.

**Example 2**
Input: `points = [[3,12],[-2,5],[-4,1]]` → Output: `18` (12 + 6)

**Example 3**
Input: `points = [[0,0]]` → Output: `0` (nothing to connect)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/min-cost-to-connect-points) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/min-cost-to-connect-all-points/)

**Network Delay Time** · Medium

A network has `n` nodes labelled `1` to `n`. `times[i] = [u, v, w]` means a signal sent from `u` reaches `v` after `w` time units (one-way). A signal starts at node `k`. Return how long it takes until **every** node has received it, or `-1` if some node can never receive it.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 100
- 1 ≤ times.length ≤ 6000, 0 ≤ w ≤ 100
- no duplicate `(u, v)` pairs

**Example 1**

```graph
2* -> 1 : 1
2* -> 3 : 1
3 -> 4 : 1
caption: signal starts at 2
```

Input: `times = [[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,4,1]], n = 4, k = 2`
Output: `2`
Nodes 1 and 3 hear it at time 1, node 4 at time 2 (via 3).

**Example 2**
Input: `times = [[1,2,1]], n = 2, k = 1` → Output: `1`

**Example 3**
Input: `times = [[1,2,1]], n = 2, k = 2` → Output: `-1` (node 1 is unreachable from 2)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/network-delay-time) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/network-delay-time/)

**Swim in Rising Water** · Hard

You get an n × n grid of distinct heights `grid[r][c]` (a permutation of `0 … n²−1`). Rain starts and at time `t` the water is at height `t` everywhere. You can swim from a cell to a neighbour (up, down, left, right) instantly, but only when **both** cells have height ≤ `t`. Starting at the top-left cell, return the earliest time at which you can reach the bottom-right cell.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ n ≤ 50
- 0 ≤ grid[r][c] < n², all values distinct

**Example 1**

```grid
0* 2
1* 3*
caption: path 0 → 1 → 3: wait until t = 3
```

Input: `grid = [[0,2],[1,3]]`
Output: `3`
The target itself has height 3, so nothing earlier than 3 can work.

**Example 2**

```grid
0* 1* 2* 3* 4*
24 23 22 21 5*
12* 13* 14* 15* 16*
11* 17 18 19 20
10* 9* 8* 7* 6*
caption: best route; its highest cell is 16
```

Input: `grid = [[0,1,2,3,4],[24,23,22,21,5],[12,13,14,15,16],[11,17,18,19,20],[10,9,8,7,6]]`
Output: `16`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/swim-in-rising-water) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/swim-in-rising-water/)

**Alien Dictionary** · Hard

An alien language uses lowercase English letters, but in an unknown order. You get a list of words that is claimed to be **sorted** by that alien order. Work out an ordering of all the letters that appear in the words that is consistent with the list and return it as a string. If no ordering can make the list sorted, return `""`. If several orderings work, return any of them.

A word that is a prefix of another must come first (`"ab"` before `"abc"`), so a longer word directly before its own prefix makes the list invalid.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 100
- 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 100, lowercase letters only

**Example 1**

```graph
w -> e
e -> r
r -> t
t -> f
caption: rules learned from neighbouring words
```

Input: `words = ["wrt","wrf","er","ett","rftt"]`
Output: `"wertf"`
`wrt`/`wrf` → t before f; `wrf`/`er` → w before e; `er`/`ett` → r before t; `ett`/`rftt` → e before r.

**Example 2**
Input: `words = ["z","x"]` → Output: `"zx"`

**Example 3**
Input: `words = ["z","x","z"]` → Output: `""` (z before x and x before z is a contradiction)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/foreign-dictionary) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/alien-dictionary/)

**Cheapest Flights Within K Stops** · Medium

There are `n` cities numbered `0 … n−1`. `flights[i] = [from, to, price]` is a one-way flight. Given a start city `src`, a destination `dst` and a number `k`, return the cheapest total price to get from `src` to `dst` with **at most `k` stops** in between (so at most `k + 1` flights). Return `-1` if no such route exists.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ n ≤ 100, 0 ≤ k < n, src ≠ dst
- 0 ≤ flights.length ≤ n·(n−1)/2, 1 ≤ price ≤ 10⁴
- no duplicate flights between the same pair, no self-loops

**Example 1**

```graph
0* -> 1 : 100
1 -> 2 : 100
2 -> 0 : 100
1 -> 3+ : 600
2 -> 3+ : 200
```

Input: `n = 4, flights = [[0,1,100],[1,2,100],[2,0,100],[1,3,600],[2,3,200]], src = 0, dst = 3, k = 1`
Output: `700`
0 → 1 → 3 costs 700 with one stop. 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 costs only 400 but needs two stops.

**Example 2**

```graph
0* -> 1 : 100
1 -> 2+ : 100
0* -> 2+ : 500
```

Input: `n = 3, flights = [[0,1,100],[1,2,100],[0,2,500]], src = 0, dst = 2, k = 1`
Output: `200` (via city 1)

**Example 3**
Input: same flights, `k = 0` → Output: `500` (only the direct flight is allowed)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/cheapest-flight-path) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/cheapest-flights-within-k-stops/)

**Climbing Stairs** · Easy

A staircase has `n` steps. Each move climbs either 1 step or 2 steps. Return the number of different sequences of moves that take you from the bottom to exactly the top.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ n ≤ 45

**Example 1**
Input: `n = 2` → Output: `2` (1+1, or 2)

**Example 2**
Input: `n = 3` → Output: `3` (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1)

**Example 3**
Input: `n = 5` → Output: `8`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/climbing-stairs) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/climbing-stairs/)

**Min Cost Climbing Stairs** · Easy

`cost[i]` is the price of standing on step `i`. You may start on step 0 or step 1 for free. From a step you pay its cost and then climb 1 or 2 steps. The top is the position just past the last step. Return the minimum total you pay to reach the top.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ cost.length ≤ 1000
- 0 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 999

**Example 1**
Input: `cost = [10,15,20]`
Output: `15`
Start on step 1, pay 15 and jump 2 steps to the top.

**Example 2**
Input: `cost = [1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1]`
Output: `6`
Step only on the 1s: indices 0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9.

**Example 3**
Input: `cost = [5,3]` → Output: `3` (start on step 1, jump to the top)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/min-cost-climbing-stairs) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/min-cost-climbing-stairs/)

**House Robber** · Medium

Houses stand in a row and `nums[i]` is the money in house `i`. You may take the money from any set of houses as long as no two chosen houses are **next to each other**. Return the largest total you can take.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 100
- 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 400

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,1]`
Output: `4`
Take houses 0 and 2: 1 + 3.

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [2,7,9,3,1]`
Output: `12`
Take houses 0, 2 and 4: 2 + 9 + 1.

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [2,1,1,2]` → Output: `4` (houses 0 and 3; skipping two in a row is allowed)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/house-robber) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/house-robber/)

**House Robber II** · Medium

Same rules as House Robber (`nums[i]` is the money in house `i`, and you can't take two neighbouring houses), but now the houses form a **circle**: the first and the last house are neighbours too. Return the largest total you can take.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 100
- 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [2,3,2]`
Output: `3`
Houses 0 and 2 are neighbours around the circle, so the best is house 1 alone.

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,1]`
Output: `4` (houses 0 and 2)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3]` → Output: `3`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/house-robber-ii) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/house-robber-ii/)

**Longest Palindromic Substring** · Medium

Given a string `s`, return its longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several have the maximum length, any one of them is accepted.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000
- `s` contains only digits and English letters

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "babad"`
Output: `"bab"`
`"aba"` is equally long and also accepted.

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "cbbd"` → Output: `"bb"` (an even-length palindrome)

**Example 3**
Input: `s = "a"` → Output: `"a"`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/longest-palindromic-substring) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-palindromic-substring/)

**Palindromic Substrings** · Medium

Given a string `s`, count how many of its substrings are palindromes (read the same both ways). Substrings at different positions count separately even if they contain the same letters.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000
- lowercase English letters only

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "abc"` → Output: `3` (`"a"`, `"b"`, `"c"`)

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "aaa"`
Output: `6`
Three single `"a"`s, two `"aa"`s (positions 0–1 and 1–2), and `"aaa"`.

**Example 3**
Input: `s = "abba"` → Output: `6` (4 single letters, `"bb"`, `"abba"`)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/palindromic-substrings) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/palindromic-substrings/)

**Decode Ways** · Medium

Letters are encoded as numbers: `A → "1"`, `B → "2"`, …, `Z → "26"`. Given a string of digits `s`, count the ways to split it into pieces that each map back to a letter. A piece can't have a leading zero (`"06"` is not a valid piece) and must be between 1 and 26. Return 0 if no split works.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 100
- `s` contains only digits (it may contain zeros)

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "12"` → Output: `2` (`1|2` = "AB", `12` = "L")

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "226"`
Output: `3`
`2|2|6`, `22|6` and `2|26`.

**Example 3**
Input: `s = "06"` → Output: `0` (a piece can't start with 0, and "0" alone isn't a letter)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/decode-ways) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/decode-ways/)

**Coin Change** · Medium

You have coin denominations `coins` (unlimited coins of each) and a target `amount`. Return the **fewest** coins whose values add up to exactly `amount`, or `-1` if it can't be done.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ coins.length ≤ 12
- 1 ≤ coins[i] ≤ 2³¹ − 1
- 0 ≤ amount ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**
Input: `coins = [1,2,5], amount = 11` → Output: `3` (5 + 5 + 1)

**Example 2**
Input: `coins = [2], amount = 3` → Output: `-1` (only even totals are reachable)

**Example 3**
Input: `coins = [1], amount = 0` → Output: `0` (no coins needed)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/coin-change) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/coin-change/)

**Maximum Product Subarray** · Medium

Given an integer array `nums`, find the non-empty contiguous subarray whose elements multiply to the **largest product**, and return that product. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2·10⁴
- −10 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [2,3,-2,4]` → Output: `6` (subarray `[2,3]`)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [-2,0,-1]` → Output: `0` (`[-2,-1]` isn't contiguous)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [-2,3,-4]` → Output: `24` (the whole array: two negatives cancel)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/maximum-product-subarray) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-product-subarray/)

**Word Break** · Medium

Given a string `s` and a list of words `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be cut into one or more pieces where every piece is a word from the list. A word may be used any number of times.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 300
- 1 ≤ wordDict.length ≤ 1000, 1 ≤ word length ≤ 20
- all lowercase; dictionary words are distinct

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "leetcode", wordDict = ["leet","code"]` → Output: `true` (`leet|code`)

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "applepenapple", wordDict = ["apple","pen"]` → Output: `true` (`apple|pen|apple`, reusing "apple")

**Example 3**
Input: `s = "catsandog", wordDict = ["cats","dog","sand","and","cat"]`
Output: `false`
`cats|and|og` and `cat|sand|og` both leave `og`, which isn't a word.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/word-break) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/word-break/)

**Longest Increasing Subsequence** · Medium

Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest **strictly increasing** subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2500
- −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]`
Output: `4`
For example `2, 3, 7, 101` (or `2, 5, 7, 18`).

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [0,1,0,3,2,3]` → Output: `4` (`0, 1, 2, 3`)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [7,7,7,7,7,7,7]` → Output: `1` (equal values aren't strictly increasing)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/longest-increasing-subsequence) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-increasing-subsequence/)

**Partition Equal Subset Sum** · Medium

Given an array of positive integers `nums`, return `true` if you can split it into two groups (every element in exactly one group) whose sums are equal.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 200
- 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 100

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [1,5,11,5]` → Output: `true` (`[1,5,5]` and `[11]`, both 11)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,5]` → Output: `false` (total 11 is odd)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [2,2]` → Output: `true`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/partition-equal-subset-sum) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/partition-equal-subset-sum/)
